title: サイバー救援隊を創設へ 政府案
body:
サイバー攻撃による個人情報の漏えいが相次ぐ事態を受け、政府が近くまとめる緊急対策パッケージの概要案が判明した。官民の専門人材からなる「官民サイバー救援隊（仮称）」を創設し、必要性が高い場合に企業や組織に派遣する。対処力を強化し、国民生活への影響を最小限に抑え込むことを目指す。【一覧表】個人情報流出が判明した企業・団体と問い合わせ先
６日にも関係閣僚会議を開き、公表する。パッケージでは、攻撃を受けても迅速に支援を受けて立ち直ることのできる「世界最高水準」の強靱（きょうじん）な社会を目指し、〈１〉ＡＩ（人工知能）を活用した対策の徹底〈２〉情報収集・分析などの体制強化〈３〉攻撃対処の戦略的実施〈４〉被害者支援・被害拡大防止――を４本柱に掲げた。
具体的には、民間の専門機関と連携し、攻撃の背景や手法などを検証する。支援の必要性が特に高い場合、企業などに同隊を派遣する調整を行うための事務局を今年度内に設置する。
海外の大手ＩＴ企業や高性能ＡＩ開発企業と協力し、攻撃につながるシステムの脆弱（ぜいじゃく）性に関する情報を早期に集約して対応の迅速化を図る。同盟・同志国と連携して国際共同捜査を推進する。

title: 仏銀行サイバー攻撃 177億円流出
body: 【AFP＝時事】フランスの地方銀行クレディ・ミュチュエル・アルケアは4日、サイバー攻撃を受け、約1億ユーロ（約177億円）に上る不正取引が行われたと発表した。【関連記事】欧州9か国のスーパー冷蔵設備にサイバー攻撃か 食品廃棄被害も同行によると、攻撃はすでに「封じ込められた」。ハッカーは同行の口座に不正アクセスし、他の銀行に送金した。顧客の口座には不正アクセスしておらず、顧客に損失は生じていない。盗まれた資金は専門の取引プラットフォームで暗号資産に換えられたが、一部は凍結され、資金の回収に向けた取り組みも進められているという。同行は、送金が人的ミスによる可能性を否定し、「外部からの巧妙な攻撃だった」と説明した。攻撃の具体的な手口や、誰が関与した可能性があるかについては、詳細を明らかにしなかった。同行は、仏紙テレグラムが報じた1億3300万ドル（約210億円）という損失額については確認を避けたが、損失の規模は認めた。また、被害額はなお精査中だが、「グループの財務の健全性や強固な財務基盤を損なう規模ではない」とした。【翻訳編集】 AFPBB News

title: 米民主党 次のリーダー不在課題
body:
【ワシントン＝栗山紘尚】３日に投開票された米中間選挙で、野党・民主党は上下両院で過半数を奪還する旋風を起こした。ただ、トランプ政権への批判票が集まった「敵失」という側面が強く、選挙戦を通じて民主党内で台頭する急進左派への対応や次世代を担うリーダーの不在など党内の課題も浮き彫りとなった。【写真】バンス副大統領「敗北の理由は戦争」
「アメリカ・イズ・バック（米国は戻ってきた）」「米国民は『うんざりだ』との明確な意思を示した」
下院民主党トップのハキーム・ジェフリーズ院内総務は３日夜、ワシントンで演説し、勝利宣言した。「自らと家族を肥やすことに夢中な政府高官の腐敗を追及する」と強調し、政権の責任を厳しく問う姿勢を示した。ジェフリーズ氏は黒人初の下院議長に就任する見通しだ。
米ＣＮＮの世論調査によると、有権者の約９割が生活費高騰を投票の決め手に挙げた。民主党はこうした有権者の声をすくい上げ、対イラン軍事作戦を始めたトランプ政権と物価高を結びつける戦略を取った。
「アフォーダビリティー（手頃な価格）」の実現を前面に打ち出したほか、トランプ氏の独善的な政権運営に対する「ブレーキ役」としての存在意義をアピールしたことも功を奏した。
トランプ氏が在任期間中に暗号資産（仮想通貨）関連で１４億ドル（約２２００億円）の収入を得たことなどを踏まえ、民主党は、トランプ氏一族が私腹を肥やしていると主張。２０２８年の大統領選に向けて、政権と与党・共和党の足元を揺さぶり、反転攻勢に弾みをつけたい考えだ。
ただ、民主党にも課題が山積している。ミシガン州の上院選で、急進左派の支援を受けて初当選を決めたアブドゥル・エルサイード氏はパレスチナ自治区ガザ情勢を巡り、「我々はジェノサイド（集団殺害）に税金が使われることを望んでいない」と述べ、イスラエルへの軍事支援の見直しを求めた。２４年の大統領選では、ガザ情勢を巡るバイデン前政権の対応が深刻な党内対立を招いており、今後のかじ取りを誤れば、再び亀裂が深まりかねない。

title: 幹部逮捕 川崎市役所を家宅捜索
body: 神奈川県川崎市の幹部が2024年、市が発注した工事の予定価格を元職員に漏らしたとして逮捕されました。【画像】マンション修繕工事171物件で談合　公取委、37社に約16億円の課徴金納付命じる警察によりますと、逮捕された川崎市まちづくり局担当部長の関口隆雄容疑者は2024年、市が発注した2つの塗装・防水工事の一般競争入札をめぐり、市の元職員で「川崎塗装業協会」の事務局長に、非公表の工事価格を漏らした疑いがもたれています。関口容疑者は当時、工事の計画などを担当する「施設整備部」の部長で、かねて付き合いがあった元職員に市役所で価格を漏えいしたあと、元職員が「川崎塗装業協会」に加盟する別の業者にも価格を伝え、入札に応募する業者を調整したとみられるということです。警察は4日、川崎塗装業協会の事務所や川崎市役所を家宅捜索していて、ほかの工事の入札でも組織的に不正がくり返されたとみて、実態解明を進めています。

title: 「哲代おばあちゃん」死去 106歳
body: 100歳を過ぎても心豊かに1人暮らしを続け、書籍やドキュメンタリー映画を通じて「哲代おばあちゃん」と親しまれてきた石井哲代（いしい・てつよ）さんが4日午後1時10分、老衰のため死去した。106歳だった。【写真】尾道映画祭にサプライズゲストとして登場した哲代さん（2026年3月）1920年4月29日、広島県府中市の出身。20歳で小学校教員になり、56歳で退職してからは、同県尾道市で畑仕事や民生委員などの地域活動に精力的に取り組んだ。子どもはなく、81歳で夫良英さんを見送った後は104歳まで1人暮らしを続けた。哲代さんの日々の暮らしぶりや、人生を明るく前向きに捉える言葉の数々は、2020年に始まった中国新聞の連載「哲代おばあちゃん　100歳きょうも好日」を通じて知られるようになった。新聞連載は書籍化されて人気は海外に広がり、ドキュメンタリー映画もヒットした。

title: イラン 大敗のトランプ氏を嘲笑
body: 【AFP＝時事】イランは4日、ドナルド・トランプ米大統領率いる共和党が中間選挙で大敗したことをあざ笑った。トランプ氏は、イランとの戦争が有権者から厳しい審判を突き付けられた主な原因だったと認めた。【写真】トランプ氏、さっそく責任逃れ「私の名前は投票用紙に載っていなかった」 中間選挙大敗でイランの首都テヘランで開かれた集会では数千人がトランプ氏を嘲笑し、同国の高官は、トランプ氏に戦略的、政治的な敗北をもたらしたのはイランだと主張した。米国とイスラエルによる攻撃で戦争が始まってから8か月。軽油や消費財の価格上昇に怒った有権者はトランプ氏率いる共和党に背を向け、同党は連邦議会の上下両院の多数派を失った。イランのモフセン・レザイ最高国家安全保障会議事務局長はX（旧ツイッター）に、「トランプに戦場とホルムズ海峡での戦略的敗北を、そしてワシントンでの政治的敗北をもたらしたのはイラン国民だ」と投稿した。テヘラン中心部では、デモ参加者らが「米国に死を」「イスラエルに死を」とシュプレヒコールを上げた。頭上には「（ガソリン）価格を決めるのはイラン国民だ」と宣言する巨大な掲示物が設置されていた。米国との和平交渉でイラン側の責任者を務めるモハマドバゲル・ガリバフ国会議長はXに、「良心に基づくものであれ、生活費の問題によるものであれ、米国民は戦争に『ノー』を突き付けた。われわれはこのメッセージを支持する」と投稿した。イランのゴラムホセイン・モホセニエジェイ司法府代表も中間選挙の結果を歓迎し、トランプ氏は「軍事的にも政治的にも敗北した」と述べた。イランの最高指導者モジタバ・ハメネイ師は、米国が攻撃を再開すれば戦火が拡大する可能性があると警告した。イランがエネルギー輸送の要衝ホルムズ海峡を封鎖したことで原油価格が急騰し、生活費の上昇につながっている。トランプ氏は、J・D・バンス米副大統領が共和党の敗因を対イラン戦争だと指摘したことについて、「おおむね正しい。戦争によってガソリン価格が高騰したからだ」と認めた。一方で、「それでも、もう一度やり直すとしても、同じことをしなければならない。長期的にはそれが唯一の答えだからだ。イランに核兵器を持たせるわけにはいかない」と述べ、対イラン軍事作戦を正当化した。中間選挙の結果により、トランプ氏が政策を実行する能力は制約を受ける可能性があるが、大統領には新たな攻撃を命じる権限が残されている。【翻訳編集】 AFPBB News

title: 米民主党 次のリーダー不在課題
body:
【ワシントン＝栗山紘尚】３日に投開票された米中間選挙で、野党・民主党は上下両院で過半数を奪還する旋風を起こした。ただ、トランプ政権への批判票が集まった「敵失」という側面が強く、選挙戦を通じて民主党内で台頭する急進左派への対応や次世代を担うリーダーの不在など党内の課題も浮き彫りとなった。【写真】バンス副大統領「敗北の理由は戦争」
「アメリカ・イズ・バック（米国は戻ってきた）」「米国民は『うんざりだ』との明確な意思を示した」
下院民主党トップのハキーム・ジェフリーズ院内総務は３日夜、ワシントンで演説し、勝利宣言した。「自らと家族を肥やすことに夢中な政府高官の腐敗を追及する」と強調し、政権の責任を厳しく問う姿勢を示した。ジェフリーズ氏は黒人初の下院議長に就任する見通しだ。
米ＣＮＮの世論調査によると、有権者の約９割が生活費高騰を投票の決め手に挙げた。民主党はこうした有権者の声をすくい上げ、対イラン軍事作戦を始めたトランプ政権と物価高を結びつける戦略を取った。
「アフォーダビリティー（手頃な価格）」の実現を前面に打ち出したほか、トランプ氏の独善的な政権運営に対する「ブレーキ役」としての存在意義をアピールしたことも功を奏した。
トランプ氏が在任期間中に暗号資産（仮想通貨）関連で１４億ドル（約２２００億円）の収入を得たことなどを踏まえ、民主党は、トランプ氏一族が私腹を肥やしていると主張。２０２８年の大統領選に向けて、政権と与党・共和党の足元を揺さぶり、反転攻勢に弾みをつけたい考えだ。
ただ、民主党にも課題が山積している。ミシガン州の上院選で、急進左派の支援を受けて初当選を決めたアブドゥル・エルサイード氏はパレスチナ自治区ガザ情勢を巡り、「我々はジェノサイド（集団殺害）に税金が使われることを望んでいない」と述べ、イスラエルへの軍事支援の見直しを求めた。２４年の大統領選では、ガザ情勢を巡るバイデン前政権の対応が深刻な党内対立を招いており、今後のかじ取りを誤れば、再び亀裂が深まりかねない。

title: 米民主党 トランプ政権監視強化へ
body: Gram Slattery　David Morgan　Jason Lange[ワシントン　４日　ロイター] - 米中間選挙で躍進した野党・民主党は４日、共和党のトランプ大統領に対する監視を強化する方針を示し、米国は向こう２年にわたり政治的な膠着状態に陥る可能性が高ま‌った。３日投開票の中間選挙では民主党が連邦議会上下両院の過半数を奪還。共和党の牙城にも食⁠い込んで幅広い勝利を収め、有権者がトランプ大統領に厳しい審判を下した形となった。共和党のトランプ氏は２０１７─２０２１年にも大統領を務めたが、民主党が支配する議会と向き合うのは今回が初めてとなる。下院民主党ト​ップのジェフリーズ院内総務は、民主党は生活費負担の軽減と政権の説明責任の追及に重点を置くと表明。「われわれはドナルド・トランプ氏のために働いているのではない。米国民‌のために働いている」とし、「下院がトランプ政権の完全な下請け機関のように機能した時代は終わった」と語った。民主党の下院過半数奪還を受け、ジェフリーズ氏は下院議長に就任する見通し。関係筋によると、共和党‌のジョンソン下院議長は下院共和党トップの少数‌党院内総務選に立候補しない意向を固めた。こうした中、トランプ大統領はこの​日、記者団をホワイトハウスに招き、自ら建設を進めるホワイトハウスのボールルーム（宴会場）を披露。トランプ氏は「『なぜホワイト‌ハウスの工事などしているのか』と批判されることがあるが、ホワイトハウスは米国を象徴する究極の存在で、完璧な状態でなければならない」とし、「私‌にとっては気分転換になる」と語った。記者団と​約１時間に及んだやり取りの中で中間選挙の結果に触れたのはわずかで、「民主党が破壊的な‌行動に出ない限り、おそらくうまくやっていけるだろう」と述べるにとどめた。ただ「私には拒否権がある」と改めて強調した。トランプ氏は⁠憲法の規定により３選を目指すことはできないが、対イラン戦争が共和党の中間選挙敗北の一因になったことを認める一方で、自らの判断は正しかったとの立場を崩さなかった。一方、２８年大統領選でトランプ氏の後継候補になる可能性があるバンス副大統領は、２月に開始した対イ⁠ラン攻撃が中間選挙での敗北の一因になったとの考えを示し、トランプ氏と一線​を画した。バンス氏はＸへ長文の投稿で「わ‌れわれが（中間選挙で）敗北した理由は戦争だ」とし、「それでも、戦争には価値があった、今後６年間にわたり上院（の多数派）を失う代償を払うだけの価値があったと主張したいなら、そうすればいい」と指摘。過去に自身が戦争終結を勧告した⁠ことについても「妥当な助言だった」とした。トランプ氏は、対イラン戦争が共和党の中間選挙での敗北の⁠一因になったと認めながらも、戦争には価値があったとの考えを表明。記者団に対し「イランの件はやらなければならなかったし、今⁠後も続けていく」と述べ、イランが核兵器を保有するのを阻止するために戦争は価値があったと主張した。バンス氏の投稿は問題視しない考えを示‌し、「その戦⁠争について言えば、私なら違う対応はしなかった」と述べ、自分自身が中間選挙の投票対象だったら勝​利していたと改めて主張。「選挙集会では信じられないほどの熱狂と支持があったが、その支持を候補者たちに移し替えることはできなかった」と語った。

title: 米大統領 民主党に「おめでとう」
body: アメリカの中間選挙で野党・民主党が上下両院で多数派の奪還を確実にしたと伝えられる中、トランプ大統領は民主党に「おめでとう」と祝意を示しました。【動画】アメリカ中間選挙 現地の様子はトランプ大統領は4日、FOXニュースのインタビューに答え、民主党が上下両院で過半数の議席を獲得したことについて「おめでとうと伝えたい。よくやったね」と述べました。そのうえで「民主党は11年間、この状況を待ち望んでいて、ようやく達成できた」と話しています。一方で、「我々はまだ終わっていない。すべての分野で歴史上、最も偉大な2年間の大領領任期を過ごしてきた」とも主張しています。

title: 米大統領 敗因巡りイラン攻撃言及
body: トランプ政権の通信簿とも言われるアメリカの中間選挙は、野党・民主党が上下両院で過半数を確実にし、トランプ政権に「NO」が突きつけられた形です。【画像】トランプ大統領がポストした赤い帽子に刺繍された文字「VETO」の意味は…最新の情勢について、ワシントンの議会前からFNNワシントン支局・林英美支局長の中継です。大手アメリカメディアは、民主党が上下両院で過半数を奪還したと報じ、民主党のシンボルカラーである青にちなんだ「ブルーウェーブが全米を覆った」と民主党の勝利を大きく伝えています。こうした中、トランプ大統領は日本時間4日午後、FOXニュースの電話インタビューに応じました。トランプ大統領は、結果について「少し驚いている。もっと良い結果が出ると思っていた」と本音を口にしました。また、敗北の理由について問われると「一因はイランだったと思う」と述べ、自身が踏み切ったイランへの軍事攻撃が影響したと話しています。イランへの攻撃後は燃料価格が高騰し、アメリカ国民の生活を直撃しました。その不満は大きく、最新の世論調査では半数以上のアメリカ人が「軍事攻撃は価値がなかった」と答えています。一方で、トランプ大統領は「議会では民主党の法案に拒否権を発動する」とも述べていて、議会運営は一筋縄ではいかなさそうです。

title: 米中間選挙 日本経済への影響は
body:
アメリカの中間選挙は民主党が上院と下院ともに勝利しました。この結果は日本にどんな影響をもたらすのでしょうか。日経平均は一時3000円以上の値下がり。今後の日本経済への「3つの影響」を見ていきます。【画像】食料品の価格はどうなる?
ステーキ＆ハンバーグの店いわたき　せんげん台店千葉健悟店長「価格が安定すればたくさんタンパク質取れるので、トランプさんよろしくお願いいたします」民主党の勝利が確実になったことで、日本にも影響が出始めています。影響がありそうなのは、原油や輸入食品など3つです。まず、原油高です。野村総合研究所　エグゼクティブ・エコノミスト木内登英氏「戦争が終結に向かえば下がる」エコノミストの木内さんは、今後、民主党が議会を占めることで、トランプ政権が求める追加の予算が認められなくなり、戦争の継続がしにくくなるとみています。「イラン攻撃前まで（原油価格は）下がらないと思いますけども、いろんな物の値段が落ちてくる」期待を寄せるのは、クリーニング店。洗濯に使う石油系溶剤から、ハンガー、仕上げのカバーまで、ナフサを使わないものはないといって良いほどです。シロヤ　あざみ野工場後藤拓也工場長「急きょもっと安いものに変えるということで、今1本9円のハンガーを使っています」ハンガーは1本12円のものから9円のものに変更するなど、企業努力を続けましたが、春にはワイシャツを1枚10円値上げしたといいます。「本当に十数年ぶり、ワイシャツの値段を上げた。この状況が落ち着いてくれると本当にありがたい」
今後、影響がありそうなのは、輸入食品です。埼玉県越谷市のステーキ店は、肉汁たっぷりのアメリカ産牛肉がウリです。ステーキは上がるのか、下がるのか。2年前、トランプ大統領が再選されたときに、店長は…。千葉店長「肉が安くなると期待。トランプさんイケイケなので（大統領に）なってくれたら」（2年前）笑顔を見せていましたが、あれから2年が経った今月4日は浮かぬ顔。「変わらないというか、少しひどくなっているかな」アメリカ産牛肉がウリのはずのステーキ店。その冷凍庫を覗くと…。「アメリカ産カルビです。他はない。切らしている」アメリカ産のストックは2ブロックだけ。円安で価格が上がったことで、卸売業者の仕入れが減ったため、店ではオーストラリア産に変更しました。「（米国産は）高すぎて客に負担がかかる」エコノミストの木内氏は、為替についてこう話します。「民主党が勝つと、やや円安ではないかなと思います。民主党は、財政の悪化に歯止めをかけるという方向を重視してます。財政の悪化リスクが小さくなるというのは通貨高要因と考えられます。ですから、ドル高・円安ということになるのではないかと思います」円安になるものの、すぐに価格に影響が出るものではないとしています。すでに影響が出ているのが、株です。下院に続き上院でも民主党が勝利したことを受けて、株価は一時3000円あまり値下がりしました。その後戻したものの、前日より800円以上安い6万2188円で、取引を終えました。今後、株価はどうなるのでしょうか。「民主党が議会を制するとAIの規制が強まるという方向で見てまして、きょうもそれもあって、株価が大幅に下がっています。アメリカのAIブームが落ちると、日本の経済にマイナスの面もあるということですね」（2026年11月4日放送分より）

title: ダウ一時1500ドル高 選挙から一夜
body: アメリカの中間選挙から一夜明け、ニューヨーク株式市場では株価が大幅に上昇しました。【写真で見る】アメリカ中間選挙「共和党」が劣勢　日本にどんな影響が？中間選挙で民主党が上下両院の過半数を獲得することが確実になったことを受け、4日のニューヨーク市場でダウ平均株価は前の日と比べて、一時、1500ドルあまり上昇しました。トランプ大統領が選挙結果を受け入れ、民主党と協力する姿勢を示したことで政治的な混乱への懸念が和らぎ、買い注文が広がりました。一方、AI関連株はデータセンターへの規制が強まるとの懸念から、一部の関連企業の株価が下落しました。また、原油市場では中東情勢の緊張緩和への期待などから、WTI原油先物価格が一時、1バレル＝87ドル台まで下落しています。

title: リニア工事費 再び増額へ検討
body:
JR東海が、リニア中央新幹線の東京・品川―名古屋間の工事費見通しを、従来の11兆円から増額する方向で検討していることが4日、関係者への取材で分かった。増額すると昨年10月以来となり、着工以降で3回目。1年ほどで再び増額を迫られる状況になった。物価上昇に伴う資材や人件費の高騰が響く。開業時期の提示に向け、改めて見積もりを進めている。金額を精査中で、年内にも公表する。【動画】リニアのホーム工事初公開　神奈川県駅
工事費見通しは11兆円でも着工した2014年時点から倍増しており、一段と事業のかじ取りの難易度が高まっていることが浮き彫りになった。鈴木康友静岡県知事が静岡工区の着工容認を今年7月に表明したのを受け、JR東海の丹羽俊介社長は品川―名古屋間の開業時期を年内に示すと説明してきた。ただ、関係者によると、開業時期を示すのが年明け以降にずれ込む可能性もあるという。静岡工区の着工は、施工に携わる大成建設がリニア談合事件を巡って国土交通省から営業停止処分を受けたのに伴い、来年3月以降の見通しとなっている。

title: 金融庁 ソニーFGに立ち入り検査
body: 金融庁は4日、複数の金銭不祥事が発覚したソニー生命保険の親会社であるソニーフィナンシャルグループ（FG）に対し、立ち入り検査に着手した。子会社へのガバナンス（企業統治）体制に不備がなかったか調べる。問題が見つかれば業務改善命令などの行政処分を検討するとみられる。プルデンシャル所長「めちゃ稼げるぞ」と後輩勧誘　裏に歪な営業組織ソニー生命は4月から全顧客約279万人の被害調査を進めている。金融庁は同社には9月から立ち入り検査を始めており、現在も続行中だ。ソニー生命をめぐっては金銭詐取や顧客から金銭を借りる不祥事が相次ぎ発覚している。持ち株会社であるソニーFGの遠藤俊英社長は元金融庁長官。グループを率いる経営トップとして、金銭不祥事を起こした子会社の内部管理体制の構築にどう関与していたのか、責任を問われることになる。（堀篭俊材）

title: ゆうちょ銀 松井証券に20%出資
body: ［東京　４日　ロイター］ - ゆうちょ銀行は４日、松井証券と資本業務提携すると発表した。松‌井証券の創業家の資産管理会社から⁠株式を取得する予定で、議決権の約２０％を保有し、持分法適用関連会社とする。株式の​譲渡実行日は１２月２８日。取得額は公表していない。幅広い顧客基盤を持つゆうち‌ょ銀と、ネット証券のパイオニアでもある松井証券の強みを合わせることで、双‌方の顧客に新たな‌価値を提供するシナジー効果が​期待できるとしている。ゆうちょ銀は、全国の郵‌便局ネットワークや口座数約１．２億に上る顧客基盤を持つ一方、株式‌やＦＸ（外国為替​証拠金取引）などの取引サービスは‌手掛けていない。松井証券との提携を通じて、金⁠融商品のラインアップや資産運用サービスを拡充し、個人向け金融サービスを強化する狙いがある。ま⁠た、子会社のゆうちょアセット​マネジメント（ＪＰＡＭ）‌が組成する資産運用商品の販売チャンネル拡充にもつながるとみている。ＪＰＡＭが運営するベンチャ⁠ーキャピタルファンドの投資先企業⁠に対し、ＩＰＯ（新規株式公開）時の引受証券会社として松井⁠証券を紹介する取り組みも進める。松井証券にとっては、‌ゆう⁠ちょ銀行の顧客基盤や郵便局ネットワー​クとの連携を通じて顧客接点の拡大が期待されるという。

title: 'This is a disaster': Angry Republicans blame Trump for midterms defeat
summary: Some Republicans tell the BBC the president's focus on his legacy and indifference to voter concerns cost them.
body:
Watch: Key moments from the US midterm election results
Inside the Republican Party, initial shock at the stunning election results on Tuesday night quickly gave way to anger with US President Donald Trump.
After Democrats won upset after upset in deep-red states like Texas, Kansas and South Carolina, some Republicans focused their ire on Trump, arguing that his focus on his legacy and indifference to voter concerns cost the party control of Congress.
"It's on him. It's not on anybody else. It's a total, complete rejection of President Trump," Bill Miller, a top Republican lobbyist in Texas, told the BBC. "This is a disaster of the first magnitude. Nobody saw it coming like this."
Most Republicans expected to lose control of the House and were clear-eyed about the challenge of holding onto the Senate in a tough election cycle that favoured the party out of power.
But some said in interviews that Trump dragged them down with unpopular policies, a low job approval rating and obsession over construction projects in Washington.
"It was just one mistake after another," said Gregg Peppin, a Republican strategist in Minnesota. "Clearly, in state after state, people did not like the president's policies."
A White House ally said public disapproval with Trump over the Iran war, tariffs and the administration's immigration crackdown created a "perfect storm" in November.
"There's palpable frustration [within] the party about how this has all played out," the person said, and much of it is directed at Trump. Anger with Trump "is extremely high".

The BBC spoke to a dozen party operatives, campaign officials, White House allies and others, many of whom spoke on background to offer a candid assessment of Trump's approach to the midterms.
Trump and Republicans had a lot riding on the outcome on Tuesday night. A stronger showing by the president's party - as happened in 2022, when Democrats under then-President Joe Biden lost just nine seats in the House, and gained one in the Senate - would have given Republicans some momentum heading into 2028.
But Trump will instead face a motivated Democratic majority in Congress that is eager to investigate the administration, block his judicial nominees and stymie the rest of his agenda.
The midterms have ushered in an uncertain new phase in Trump's second term and may force Republicans to start grappling with their post-Trump future.
The result amounted to a rejection of Trump, one top Republican lobbyist said
"I don't think his influence is slipping," said Steve Scheffler, the Republican National Committeeman in Iowa, speaking on the eve of the election. Still, he said, when it came to the midterms, "there were things you wish he said differently".
Trump was silent for much of the night before posting a message on Truth Social after the House and Senate were called for Democrats.
"I wasn't on the Ballot and if I was, we would have won IN A LANDSLIDE! Thank you for your attention to this matter," Trump wrote.
He said in later interviews with the New York Times and Fox News that he would accept the election results. Trump told Fox he was a "little bit surprised" by the election results, but noted that the president's party typically fared poorly in midterm elections.
Republican Senator Jon Husted at an election event in Ohio, where the Senate seat flipped in favour of Democrat Sherrod Brown
Since 1934, the party in the White House has only gained seats in three midterm elections. While the Democratic gains in 2026 did not set a record, the party did win dozens of House races, state governor contests and Senate seats, including in states where the party had not been competitive for decades.
Before Tuesday, Democrats had not won a Senate seat in Kansas since 1932, and had not won a statewide race in Texas in more than three decades. The party also notched surprise upsets in other reliably red states like South Carolina that were thought to be safe seats for Republicans just weeks before Election Day.
Trump and Vice-President JD Vance held dozens of campaign rallies in the run-up to the midterms. The principal Trump-aligned Super PAC, MAGA Inc., spent hundreds of millions backing Republican candidates.
Trump allies said it was unfair to hold him responsible for the party's election losses. They pointed to the history of midterm elections, and said the party was saddled with weak Republican candidates in battleground states like Georgia, Michigan and Texas.
Ken Paxton, the Republican Senate nominee in Texas, ran "the worst Senate campaign in the country from either side of the aisle," said another Texas Republican operative, who spoke on the condition of anonymity. "If Ken's campaign knocked on 100,000 doors I'd be shocked," the source said. The person added that Paxton's victorious Democratic opponent, James Talarico, ran "a really good and smart campaign."
Democrats 'got their wish': Voters react to midterm results
Others defended Trump's autumn campaign schedule, noting that he had to balance his day job of running the country with midterm travel.
"He's the president. He's not going to spend his time campaigning 24/7," said Krish Mathrani, the Michigan Republican Party's youth chair. Mathrani said Trump's campaign rallies helped drive up enthusiasm among Republican voters. "President Trump is a turnout machine," he said.
That's true in presidential elections. But Trump's vaunted turnout operation has failed to deliver in elections when he's not on the ballot, and 2026 proved no different.
Voters rejected Trump's argument that the economy was better on his watch and that he was achieving his aims in the war with Iran. The effort by Trump to portray Democrats as extreme socialists also fell flat, as voters handed victories to moderates like Roy Cooper in North Carolina.
"That just didn't work with Cooper," said a Cooper campaign official. "Trying to tag him as some socialist liberal, that wasn't going to fly."
Republican supporters at a watch party in Iowa, where Democrat candidate Josh Turek won a Senate seat
Trump often seemed disinterested in the midterms over the summer, the period of time when Republicans in Congress shifted their focus to the election.
Trump was consumed by the war with Iran abroad and his construction overhaul of Washington at home. The projects included the under-construction ballroom and a helipad on the South Lawn of the White House, renovations to a local golf course, a proposed memorial arch near Arlington Cemetery and renovations to the Kennedy Center.
Events like a UFC match at the White House on Trump's 80th birthday in June created the impression that the president was more interested in feting himself than winning the midterms, several sources said. Trump also repeatedly downplayed the rising costs of gas and often cast the affordability issue as a Democratic hoax.
Trump turned his full attention to the election in September at the Republican Party's midterm convention. The event was a gamble: Republicans hadn't held a midterm convention in decades, and it was an open question whether voters would tune in.
Trump dominated the convention in Dallas, frustrating Republicans who told the BBC they wanted to highlight the party's midterm candidates.
In his rambling keynote speech, Trump pledged to give $5,000 (£3,700) to Americans if Republicans retained control of Congress and raised eyebrows with an endorsement of Paxton which included a lengthy criticism of the candidate's lack of charisma and physical appearance.
"Obviously, that's never helpful," Robin Armstrong, Texas' Republican National Committeeman, said of Trump's critique of Paxton. "You're not going to stop what President Trump says. We just have to kind of live with that."
The convention failed to attract a large television audience, and Democrats were quick to call it a failure. "It backfired for Republicans because nobody paid any attention to it," said Terri Burke, the Texas Democratic Party's executive director.
Trump's penchant for straying off-message continued when he hit the campaign trail in the final weeks before Election Day. He made headlines for praising Ohio Republican Senator John Husted's physique, and drew criticism for calling Abdul El-Sayed a "jihadist" in the Michigan Senate race.
Mike Rogers in Michigan was among the other losing candidates - having been beaten to a Senate seat by Democrat Abdul El-Sayed
As Trump criss-crossed the country stumping for Republican candidates, the White House contended with controversies in Washington. Katie Zacharia was ousted after just five days as White House press secretary, and Kimberly Guilfoyle resigned as the US ambassador to Greece after reports surfaced that she asked a donor to pay her credit card debt.
Trump also faced a backlash in October for striking a deal to buy Russian diesel. The agreement, which blindsided members of Congress and drew condemnation from some Republicans, came just weeks after Trump signed a sanctions bill aimed at cutting off Russian oil and gas revenue.
Democrats used the deal and other scandals swirling around the White House to make the case for retaking control of Congress. The messaging resonated in the end, as Democrats flipped both chambers of Congress in convincing fashion.
A second White House ally said that the president's political aides projected optimism until the final days of the election, even as it became clear the party was headed to defeat.
Now, as Republicans take stock of the loss, several said they were ready to look ahead to the 2028 election.

title: US midterm results a 'victory' for Canadians hopeful of tariff relief
summary: With Canada-US trade talks back on, Tuesday’s midterm Democratic wave puts pressure on the White House to come to a deal.
body:
US tariffs on Canada featured heavily in Michigan and Maine, where Democratic candidates won big on Tuesday
It was the midterm result that many in Canada had hoped for - a Democratic sweep that was in part a repudiation by American voters of Donald Trump's tariff on close trade allies.
"I was doing cartwheels down the street," said Ontario Premier Doug Ford on Wednesday morning, calling it "a victory for Canada".
Tuesday night's result is unlikely to grant Canada relief from those tariffs any time soon, but there is anticipation that the political shifts could create a more favourable environment for Ottawa to get the best deal now that on-again-off-again trade talks are back on.
US voters cited affordability as a main concern heading into the midterms and asurvey by the Cato Institute in September,externalsuggested that about 75% believe the tariffs have raised prices.
In states like Maine and Michigan, tariffs played a significant role in the hard-fought races.
In Maine, incumbent Republican Senator Susan Collins clashed with the White House over tariffs.
She successfully lobbied to have some duties that directly affected the state removed, including on road salt, refrigeration equipment and seaweed, but in the end lost to Democrat Troy Jackson.
A similar story played out in Michigan, where state's the automobile manufacturing industry is deeply intertwined with Canada's - and where Democratic candidate Abdul El-Sayed defeated Republican Mike Rogers.

In Ohio, Senator-elect Sherrod Brown, who defeated Republican Jon Husted,called the levies a "disaster" and vowed to slash costs for voters by getting rid of them,external.
Democratic leaders like Hakeem Jeffries and Chuck Schumer, now newly empowered, have both pushed to rein in the tariffs on Canada in recent months.
Still, Democratic control of Congress might not do much to move the needle on tariffs. Trump's levies have been largely enacted using executive orders without approval from Congress.
And speaking to Fox News on Tuesday night, Trump touted his "ultimate power" of veto to shut down bills passed by Congress that he does not like.
Some Democratic lawmakers have also supported certain tariffs in the past as a way to protect American manufacturing jobs, and could back keeping some in place.
How the Democratic takeover of the Senate could impact Trump
There are currently several layers of tariffs on Canada, notably on sectors like autos, steel, aluminium and forestry.
After trade talks between Ottawa and Washington collapsed in August, the Trump administration imposed an additional 50% tariff on $20bn (£15bn) worth of various Canadian goods, from dairy to cosmetics and furniture.
The US also declared a total import ban on motorcycles, whey protein and alcohol.
Canada retaliated by slapping the US with its own 50% "dollar-for-dollar" tariffs. Most provinces have also banned the sale of US alcohol in retaliation.
Trump had also previously threatened to escalate the trade war with Canada further by ⁠raising tariffs on sectors, including auto manufacturing, as of 1 January.
There were signs that his administration had become more sensitive to the optics of its tariffs on Canada in the run up to the election.
Just a few days before the vote, Trump told reporters that a trade deal is "very close" after speaking with Prime Minister Mark Carney.
Speaking to reporters on Tuesday evening, Carney said of US negotiators that "they're asking less and they're offering more" in recent discussions.
On Wednesday, US-Canada Trade Minister Dominic LeBlanc said the midterm results won't change anything in the short term, and dismissed speculation over  what the new Congress might do when they're seated in the new year as "an interesting discussion at a faculty club luncheon".
"Our approach will not change and we don't intend to speculate on the approach being taken by the Americans," he said.
Pierre Poilievre, leader of Canada's Conservatives, said on Wednesday that "nobody controls Donald Trump".
But he said that midterms results show Canada has "massive leverage" given that the tariffs are broadly unpopular.
"We've got to use that goodwill to pressure for tariff-free trade," he said.
Watch: Key moments from the US midterm election results
Trump may indeed feel more pressure to sign a deal with Canada now that American voters have clearly communicated their frustration, said Colin Robertson, a former Canadian diplomat and a fellow at the Canadian Global Affairs Institute.
"Will this change Trump's mind? It might, because he suffered such a beating at the polls."
But he added it remains to be seen how Trump will react from the bruising midterm loss.
Canada has an ideal window between now and January - when the new Democratic lawmakers are sworn in - to finalise a deal, Robertson noted.
After that, Trump is likely to be distracted by investigations launched by Democrats into Trump's family and finances and some members of his administration, Robertson said.
US trade representative Jamieson Greer also said earlier this year that he had ambitions to have interim deals in place with Canada and Mexico around the North American free trade deal, known as the USMCA in the US and CUSMA in Canada, before the end of the year.
And while Carney struck a more optimistic tone in recent days on the current state of Canada-US trade talks, he also told Politico last month that he was prepared to wait for a new American president if necessary to reach a deal with the US.

title: Ukraine says bodycam video shows deadly Russian double-tap bombing
summary: At least 40 people were killed and another 30 may still be under the rubble after Monday's attack on a Ukrainian village, Kyiv says.
body:
Video shows moments between deadly Russian attacks on village in Ukraine
A bodycam video has been released by Ukraine police which they say shows the moments between two powerful Russian bomb strikes that killed at least 40 people at an aid centre and a shelter.
The footage, from a camera on one of the killed police officers, shows residents of the southern village of Kamyshuvakha going to an underground shelter after the first attack on Monday. Soon after a blast is heard and flames are seen as the shelter is hit.
President Volodymyr Zelensky said more than 30 people may still be under the rubble, as a search operation continued for the third day.
Nine gliding bombs, some weighing 3,000kg, hit the village as people had gathered to get humanitarian aid, Ukraine said.
Search efforts are continuing after the Russian bombing completely destroyed the shelter in Kamyshuvakha, leaving a huge crater
The bodycam footage was released by Ukraine's national police on Wednesday.
It shows huge devastation after the first bomb strike on the village in Ukraine's Zaporizhzhia region, as shocked local residents stare at the rubble.
Severely damaged buildings are also seen.
A voice of a military official is then heard on a two-way radio warning police on the ground of more glide bombs being launched towards Kamyshuvakha.
"Quickly [go] to the shelter!" one of the police officers tells local residents, who are seen walking into the shelter - at least two floors underground.
Seconds later the shelter is hit, and the recording stops.
Ukraine said the shelter was near a local school, which was being used to distribute humanitarian aid.
BBC Verify has confirmed the video was filmed in the same place as footage released by the Ukrainian state emergencies service DSNS showing the aftermath Monday's attack in Komyshuvakha.
In a post on social media on Wednesday, Zelensky said that "nine aerial bombs were dropped by the Russians.
"First, they hit people who came to receive humanitarian aid, and then rescuers and police officers who arrived at the scene."
The Ukrainian president added that "unfortunately, there has been very little reaction from the world to this insane attack", describing it as yet another of "thousands" of war crimes committed by Russia.
Ukraine's DSNS earlier posted another video showing a huge crater left after the attack on Kamyshuvakha.
The Russian military has not publicly commented.
Russian President Vladimir Putin launched a full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022.
In a separate development on Wednesday, Zelensky said he talked "in great detail for an hour-and-a-half" with US President Donald Trump's peace envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner ahead of trilateral negotiations between Ukraine, Russia and the US on 10-11 November in Abu-Dhabi.
The Ukrainian leader - who is currently making a surprise visit to Spain - also said his team had a separate "meaningful" meeting in Brussels with representatives from the US, the EU, France, Britain, Germany, as well as Nato and the World Bank about "post-war reconstruction".
He added that the meeting in Belgium's capital would continue on Thursday to discuss "security guarantees" for Ukraine.
Since the trilateral talks aimed at ending the war were suspended in February, Moscow has stepped up attacks as Kyiv virtually ran out of Western-supplied interceptors to defend against missiles.
Analysts expect no major breakthrough when the talks resume in the capital of the United Arab Emirates.

title: French blood storage impacted by freezer hacks as theories swirl about culprits
summary: The French Blood Establishment (EFS) said cold rooms storing blood were impacted by hackers.
body:
French authorities say that fridges used in medical facilities to store blood for donations were impacted by recent cyber-attacks by unknown hackers.
The French Blood Establishment (EFS) said cold rooms storing blood were impacted by hackers, with temperatures set to rise - but staff intervened to protect blood supplies.
"No health impact has been identified and no loss of blood products is to be reported," the EFS said.
Up until now, only supermarkets were known to have been impacted by the hacks.
Meanwhile rumours have been circulating online about Russian hacktivist groups claiming they worked together to hack one of the systems that was used in the attacks which have affected European supermarkets.
Noname057(16) and Z-Pentest Alliance posted that they successfully hacked Danfoss which led to speculation that they were the culprits behind the freezer hacks.
But analysts now question whether or not that meant they were behind the supermarket cyber-attacks.
While Russian groups are not being ruled out, experts say Iranian hacktivists or nation state hackers - or even teenagers pulling pranks - could also be the culprits.
Cyber-security researchers at multiple firms are poring over evidence gathered from so-called "honeypots" to provide clues as to who is behind the waves of freezer hacks.
Three separate cyber-security firms have deployed fake freezer software traps to monitor how hackers attempt to use them for attacks.
In cyber-security, a "honeypot" is a digital decoy - such as a fake computer network or file - deliberately set up to look like a vulnerable target to lure and trap hackers.
By monitoring these traps, security experts can safely study an attacker's methods without putting real systems at risk.
According to activity gathered after the first wave of cyber-attacks, the second wave which hit several European countries was highly targeted.
"The fact that all these fridge freezers were hit simultaneously suggests planning and coordination," says Ryan Dewhurst from Spanish cyber-security company Previdian.
The entry point to the affected freezer software products was not difficult to exploit as they were poorly protected, with known attack methods already floating around online.
But experts like Dewhurst say the hacker or hackers had to gather the information about the devices' public IP addresses to create a target list then take time to plan which methods to use and when to execute them.
"Given the reported timing of when the devices had their temperatures increased, which seems to have been overnight for maximum damage - this is further evidence that the attack was planned and co-ordinated," he said.
Another cyber firm which has deployed similar honeypot tech to lure the hackers into revealing their tactics is Strathclyde-based Lupovis.
It had honeypots which appeared to be located around the world, and started seeing activity 10 days before the second wave of cyber-attacks.
Intriguingly, the team saw hackers scanning and probing their fake freezer sites only in Europe.
"We saw none of our honeypots in places like Africa or South America targeted at all," said Lupovis founder Dr Xavier Bellekens.
"Even pots in Ukraine were left alone."
A third company - French cyber-defence firm Sekoia - also noticed scanning activity prior to the second wave of cyber-attacks, but said it could have been automatic scanning without malicious intent.
In a report to its customers, it said evidence suggested the nature of the attack aligned with activity of Russian hacktivists or the Russian government, which is being accused of carrying out so-called "hybrid warfare" cyber-attacks across Europe.
But Sekoia's research also points to Iranian regime hackers or hacktivists too.
"Iranian-aligned actors have an established record of targeting internet-exposed industrial control systems and previous incidents involved the same equipment in Israel and the US - both adversaries of Iran," the report said.
According to Sekoia, about 40 Israeli supermarkets running Danfoss controllers were compromised back in 2022.
Meanwhile in late August, freezers in at least six US military bases were forced into defrost mode, as in France. The controller models remain unconfirmed and investigations are ongoing.
"To date, we have no technical evidence indicating the involvement of Russian-speaking groups," a Sekoia spokesperson told the BBC.
"Furthermore, as NoName057 is not known to effectively conduct operations beyond DDoS attacks and has a history of making false attributions, we remain sceptical of their alleged claim of responsibility."
Distributed denial of service (DDoS) attacks work by flooding a website or online service with internet traffic in an attempt to throw it offline, or otherwise make it inaccessible.
Authorities in several countries are actively investigating the hacks and warning supermarkets about potential future attacks.
But no formal attribution has been made.
None of the three cyber firms which have been gathering honey pot data are ruling out that it could be a teenager.
But with the degree of planning necessary the experts all agree it would have to be a well co-ordinated group - and if so, they would expect online bragging to surface soon.
Sekoia also said the possibility remains that all three waves could have been carried out by different and distinct groups or copycats.

title: 'Most difficult days of my life' for keeper Owono
summary: FC Andorra goalkeeper Jesus Owono puts out a statement through his club, expressing his sorrow and pain after Tenerife forward Jesus de Miguel's death.
body:
Fans pay respects to Tenerife's De Miguel
FC Andorra goalkeeper Jesus Owono says he is experiencing "the most difficult days of my life" after the death of Tenerife forward Jesus de Miguel.
Tenerife player De Miguel, 30,died after suffering a serious injury in a collision with Owonoduring a Spanish second division match on Monday.
The world of football has paid tribute to De Miguel, a father-of-one who joined Tenerife in summer 2025, with a minute's silence being held at all games in European competition this week.
Owono's club issued a statement on the goalkeeper's behalf on Wednesday, explaining the 25-year-old "wishes to share a few words personally".
"These are the most difficult days of my life," Owono says in the statement.
"I struggle to find the words, and it is very hard for me to come to terms with what has happened.
"I feel enormous pain over the loss of Jesus. I think of him, his family, and everyone who loved him.
"I know there will be many issues to address, and I will face whatever comes with the utmost respect. But right now, honestly, I cannot think about anything other than Jesus and the pain we are all experiencing.
"Rest in peace, Jesus."
Earlier on Wednesday, FC Andorra team-mate Lautaro Spatz defended Owono and said he "would never intentionally hurt anyone" and had been "deeply affected" by De Miguel's death.
Writing on social media, centre-back Spatz said Owono was devastated.
Spatz paid tribute to De Miguel, then said of Owono: "Those of us who know him know the kind of person he is, how much he is suffering at this moment and that he would never intentionally hurt anyone.
"In football, unfortunate incidents can happen but no-one could imagine that one of them might end with such tragic consequences."
Players from FC Andorra held a minute's silence before a voluntary training session on Wednesday. Owono was not at the session.
Football world mourns Tenerife striker De Miguel
Tenerife and Andorra were drawing 2-2 seven minutes into stoppage time on Monday when the incident occurred.
Owono ran towards the centre circle to clear a long ball when his knee appeared to collide with De Miguel.
The striker lay motionless on the pitch as medical staff treated him, before he was taken by ambulance from Tenerife's Estadio Heliodoro Rodriguez Lopez to hospital.
Owono was sent off and the match was abandoned.
The goalkeeper, who had over 30,000 followers on Instagram on Tuesday morning, has since deactivated his account.
Police in Spain opened a routine investigation into possible involuntary manslaughter following De Miguel's death.
Under Spanish law, any death that is deemed non-natural automatically triggers a judicial inquiry.
Owono has made 47 international appearances for Equatorial Guinea.
The president of Equatorial Guinea's football federation, Venancio Tomas Micha, issued a statement on Tuesday offering "all our human and professional backing" to the player.
"As the involuntary protagonist of this tragic incident in the game, he is living through this situation with deep sorrow and distress," he added.
Jesus de Miguel joined Tenerife in 2025 on a three-year deal
On Tuesday, mourners laid flowers and lit candles beneath a black and white image of De Miguel at the Estadio Heliodoro Rodriguez Lopez.
Tenerife said in a statement they will commence six official days of mourning, with all club activities suspended during this time.
The club's players, staff and officials will attend De Miguel's funeral, which will take place in Navahermosa, Toledo.
Tenerife will also open their home ground on Saturday evening to allow supporters to "bid a fitting farewell".
"Jesus de Miguel's family would like to thank everyone for their messages of support and, from the bottom of their hearts, ask that their privacy be respected at this terrible time. May he rest in peace," added the club statement.
Tenerife and Andorra's Spanish second division matches scheduled for the weekend, against Granada and Mallorca respectively, have been postponed.

title: Interest rates expected to rise for first time in over three years
summary: Most analysts are predicting an increase from 3.75% to 4%, the first increase in more than three years.
body:
Policymakers at the Bank of England are expected to raise interest rates on Thursday in what would be the first increase to the benchmark rate for more than three years.
Most analysts are predicting an rise from 3.75% to 4% in a move that would increase the cost of borrowing for individuals and businesses, but boost savers.
The Bank rate has fallen from its 2023-24 peak of 5.25%, although the Bank's Monetary Policy Committee (MPC) has left the rate unchanged at its last six meetings.
Rising inflation, driven primarily by the cost of petrol and diesel, will push policymakers into an interest rate hike, analysts suggest.
The announcement will be made by the Bank at 12:00 GMT on Thursday.
Close attention will also be paid to any hints from the MPC on the future direction of interest rates.
"The decision is increasingly less about whether rates reach 4% and more about what follows after that," said Chris Cheverall, head of UK at trading platform CMC Markets.
"A quarter-point rise is already widely expected, but the Bank now has to balance inflation that is still too high against an economy where the growth outlook has weakened sharply."
The Consumer Prices Index (CPI) measure of inflation is well below its peak of a few years ago but has been heading back up and is expected to go higher.
It was3.5% in the year to September 2026, up from 3.1% the previous month and well above the central bank's 2% target.
The ongoing impact of the Iran war, primarily on the cost of energy and fuel, has filtered through to the UK inflation rate. Millions of domestic energy customers are braced for a hefty rise in prices in January.
The Bank of England last raised rates in August 2023.
Its base rate is what it charges other banks and building societies to borrow money, which influences what they charge their own customers for mortgages as well as the interest rate they pay on savings.
Were the Bank rate to rise, there would be an immediate impact on the 510,000 tracker mortgage-holders.
A 0.25 percentage point rise would mean a £31 increase in monthly repayments for someone with a typical tracker home loan, according to calculations by banking trade body UK Finance.
The 470,000 mortgage-holders on variable deals would need to wait for their lender's reaction to any Bank rate rise. Typically, a 0.25 percentage point rise would mean a £14 increase per month in repayments.
The picture for those on fixed deals is more nuanced.
While their monthly payments are not immediately affected by a rate change, their future deals are, and lenders have already "priced in" the expected rate rise when quoting new deals.
As of 4 November, the average two-year fixed residential mortgage rate was 5.96%, while the average five-year rate stood at 5.99%, according to financial information service Moneyfacts.
It means anyone rolling off a five-year deal faces a much bigger mortgage bill.
Broker L&C said that average mortgage rates offered by the 10 biggest lenders suggested some borrowers now faced paying almost £5,000 more each year in repayments on a £200,000 mortgage over 25 years than those who secured a remortgage deal in 2021.
Five years ago, the average five-year fixed remortgage rate among the 10 biggest lenders was 1.30%.
Relatively high fixed rates have prompted some people to consider choosing trackers, in the hope that the rate would be lower, even if the Bank rate rises in the coming months.
"The right choice ultimately depends on borrowers being confident they can stomach future rises. The devil is in the detail," said Rachel Springall from Moneyfacts.
The cost of some other new loans could be influenced by the Bank rate.
Savers, on the flipside, could see the interest rates offered to them improve in light of any rise in the Bank rate.
Ultimately, lenders - as well as policymakers at the Bank of England - are having to judge what may happen to the UK's economic outlook which is highly connected to changes in international events.

title: Pound rises to its highest level since the Brexit referendum
summary: Pound reaches highest level against a basket of currencies since the Brexit referendum a decade ago
body:
The pound has risen to its highest overall level since the Brexit referendum over a decade ago.
Sterling has risen notably in recent weeks against the euro and the dollar, ahead of an expected rise in interest rates.
The most-watched measure of the value of the British currency against a basket of 18 of the world's main currencies this week reached its joint highest level since the June 2016 referendum, according to Bank of England figures.
The value reached 86.4 on an index where 100 equals the value in 2005. The Bank will officially confirm the calculation on Thursday.
The value of sterling fell significantly after the Brexit referendum in June 2016, and reached further lows during the Brexit process, the Covid pandemic and the 2022 mini-Budget.
Some traders said the UK was being seen in a different light given relative political stability, solid growth and the rapprochement with the European Union.
Sterling has responded strongly to Brexit developments and political uncertainty in recent years.
Jim O'Neill, an economist and former Treasury minister, said: "I'm not surprised. People were, and to a lesser extent, are, underestimating the improving momentum in the UK,"
A stronger pound can help rein in inflation, and increase buying power for consumers on imports and on holidays.
UK growth so far this year has outperformed all forecasts, but there are signs that higher energy and fuel prices have now hit consumer confidence.
The Bank's nine member Monetary Policy Committee faces an important decision on interest rates on Thursday, with the first rise in three years widely expected.
On Wednesday sterling was up 0.28% against the dollar at $1.3434 and was flat against the euro at €1.1996 as of 23:01 GMT.

title: Elon Musk's millions failed to deliver Republican wins in fierce midterms
summary: Musk spent nearly $500m in the 2026 US midterm elections, an individual election spending record.
body:
Watch: Key moments from the US midterm election results
Elon Musk spent almost $450m (£334m) – more than anyone ever has in an election cycle – to back Republican political candidates in the US midterm races. It was not enough to keep Democrats from aresounding victory.
Among the most striking wins went to Democrat James Talarico, who beat Republican Ken Paxton for a US Senate seat in Texas. Musk spent at least $45m in support of Paxton, according to aBBC analysis of campaign finance data.
Other races where Musk spent millions included Arizona, Michigan, Wisconsin and Minnesota. His spending continued into Monday, records show.
By Tuesday night, Musk seemed to admit defeat, joking on X that his "election-interfering space lasers didn't work."

The loss this week of so many Republican seats may have significant implications for Musk and his businesses.
SpaceX has gained anestimated,external$10bn in new government contracts since Trump was elected to his second non-consecutive term. Several democratic lawmakers have said the company's extensive and growing role in government and national securityshould be investigated,external.
SpaceX's future development of massive data centres is also facing new potential difficulties - as are the data centre developments of other tech companies.
In Georgia for instance, where SpaceX has data centre operations, the just elected Democratic governorran in-part on limiting the rapid rise of the massive buildings, as well as the huge tax breaks tech companies usually get to build them.
A number of other politicians ran on limiting data centres and dozens of state measures to limit their developmentpassed on Tuesday,external.
Data centres are sprawling buildings that house stacks of computing hardware. Tech and artificial intelligence (AI) companies use them to run online platforms such as ChatGPT, Claude, and Musk's X and his AI company xAI.
Musk posted to X on Tuesday that his previously floated idea to somehow build data centres in space was "looking pretty appealing right now."
Five reasons why Republicans lost so badly
Democrats won Congress in a blue wave. Now comes the hard part.
Tech companies involved in AI may be in for a tougher government scrutiny and potential regulation with Democrats in power, though any legislation would need Trump's approval.
James Flintoft, head of investment solutions at AJ Bell, pointed to Musk's unsuccessful spending on Republican candidates and the scale of wins by Democrats as bringing in a "period of uncertainty for investors as they assess whether tech companies are set to face greater regulation."
Senator Ed Markey on Wednesday responded on X to a person asking if major tech industry executives would be the target of investigations, saying: "They are going to need to plant new forests for all of the subpoenas we'll be printing."
Tech stocks were broadly up on Wednesday morning. Yet, Musk's Tesla and SpaceX were down by 4.9% and 3.4% respectively.
By Wednesday, Musk had stopped posting to X about politics and was instead posting in praise of GrokBot, an AI chatbot produced by xAI. It was a stark contrast to the 2025 election, when Musk would post to X sometimes hundreds of times in a day about politics.
He also unpinned a post that had been saved to the top of his X profile since last week that explained his "concern" with Democratic politicians winning more midterm races.
Those concerns included the idea that the US could welcome more immigrants, make Washington DC and Puerto Rico individual states, and expand the number of justices on the Supreme Court.
Another post telling his 241 million X followers to "Vote red today!" appeared on Wednesday to have been deleted from Musk's profile.
The BBC has contacted SpaceX for comment about Musk's spending and posts.
While Musk spent millions of dollars backing Republican candidates in multiple US states, a lot of his political focus seemed to be on Texas.
In recent years, Musk made the state the corporate headquarters of Tesla and SpaceX, both of which still have large operations in California where they were founded.
"There is something deeply wrong with Talarico", Musk posted to X in October.
Talarico posted in response: "There is something deeply wrong with a political system that allows one trillionaire to buy his own personal US Senator."
Not all billionaires in the US shared Musk's preference for Republicans.
Reid Hoffman, a tech billionaire and the founder of LinkedIn who is a major donor to Democrats, hailed the results of Tuesday's elections as an event that "blew the doors off our expectations."
"These elections were an overwhelming wave against Trump and his cronies," Hoffman wrote on X and on LinkedIn. "While people like Elon are spending outrageous amounts to keep authoritarian clowns in power, those of us who believe in the ideals of America cannot yield."

title: Poundland owner in crunch talks as retailer's collapse looms
summary: Gordon Brothers will meet Jonathan Reynolds on Wednesday as the investment firm faces scrutiny over Poundland.
body:
Business Secretary Jonathan Reynolds has met the US-based owners of Poundland as the government hopes to save the retailer from collapse.
The discount chain is on the brink of insolvency and Gordon Brothers, which bought it for £1 last June, has rejected a takeover bid which could have saved the 12,000 jobs currently at risk.
A meeting was due to be held on Thursday but has been brought forward as the scramble to secure a rescue deal for the firm intensifies.
Gordon Brothers has previously said Poundland faces multiple economic challenges from rising inflation, increasing staff costs, and "severe levels of shoplifting".
Both Reynolds and Prime Minister Andy Burnham have questioned why a deal for the future of the business has not been made.
On Wednesday, a source close to business secretary said Reynolds "has been firm that Gordon Brothers must do everything in their power to protect jobs and provide certainty for workers".
"He is pleased to have secured this commitment from Gordon Brothers in the meeting and will continue to hold the company to account and closely monitor developments," the source added.
It is understood that Gordon Brothers made a commitment in the meeting to prioritise bids that will protect workers and units.
However, it is still unclear whether the US investment firm will keep the business together or break it up.
Meanwhile, MPs say they have called in Poundland's owners for questioning on Wednesday 11 November to explain their role in the discount retailer's looming insolvency.
Liam Byrne, chair of Parliament's business committee, said: "Every report suggests Poundland is a viable, profitable business with a future ahead of it and without good reason to let it crash and burn - and then to break it up and sell it off piece by piece.
"We are asking Gordon Brothers to appear before Parliament to explain themselves and tell us just what it is that's preventing them from accepting the fully-funded deal on the table to save more than 12,000 jobs."
Business Minister Kate Dearden and union representatives met Poundland's managing director Barry Williams on Wednesday.
Mr Williams told the BBC that Poundland is profitable and sales were growing.
"We're back in profit and it has a bright future ahead of it if it's allowed to deliver that," he said.
Poundland has filed a notice of intention to appoint administrators, which protects it from its creditors until next Thursday.
Adam Turner: We would lose "a few million" if Poundland went under
Asked what his message for Poundland's owner was, Burnham said Gordon Brothers should "focus on the people in your employment" and "come up with a practical solution that saves jobs and saves those stores".
"There is a solution to be found here, sit down with us and let's find it," he added.
The meeting comes after a major Poundland supplier has said it will lose millions of pounds if the retailer goes bust.
Adam Turner, sales director at Bradford-based Highcrest Retail Brands, said Poundland was one of its biggest customers and its collapse would cost it "a few million" in lost sales.
The family owned business mainly sells confectionery to Poundland and turns over about £50m.
Turner said the firm becoming insolvent would leave a substantial gap in its balance sheet next year.
Highcrest was a "longstanding business that can stomach this", Turner said. But he warned other medium and small suppliers to the retailer have told him that "if Poundland goes under, so do they".
This echoes awarning from Poundland founder Steve Smithon Monday that two or three thousand suppliers to the firm, which only work for Poundland, would be directly affected by its collapse.
Not only would Poundland's 12,000 staff be affected in that case, but potentially up to 30,000 overall, he told the BBC on Wednesday.
He said he was "amazed" Poundland was being put into administration, pointing to the profitability of the company.
"Also, there's two offers on the table from some really good people," he added.
"All I'm asking is for Gordon Brothers to see if they can put a deal together."
Gordon Brothers said Walsall-based Poundland is "still not cash generative at a sustainable level" because of the economic issues it faces.
If Poundland's stores are sold to new buyers, some of the employees may get new jobs on the same premises.
However, it is understood that buyers are only interested in about half the stores at present – meaning roughly 6,000 employees would not be re-employed.
Poundland's founder offers to invest in firm
If Poundland goes under, suppliers will be getting "pennies in the pound" back from the administration, he said, which is "very upsetting" – although he still hopes a deal can be done so Poundland can remain solvent.
Poundland owners Gordon Brothers will be a secured creditor, which means they are first in line to get their money back, and suppliers "who have done nothing wrong" will take the financial hit.
"It's sad. It's a nightmare for us all to be honest with you. It's not just the suppliers, it's the staff at Poundland, some of these guys have been there for many years.
"It's from the warehouse staff all the way to the shop staff to everybody within head office. It's a massive ripple effect through the supply chain," he added.
Turner said he had no knowledge of whether Gordon Brothers had deliberately timed the process of Poundland going into administration so it could take advantage of having high stock levels, which it can then sell.
One of the ways Gordon Brothers makes money is through stock liquidations – selling off stock from collapsed businesses.
One insider familiar with the situation told the BBC that the timing of Poundland facing collapse was "odd" – most retailers don't fall over in the run-up to Christmas.
Dearden has said the government doesn't want to interfere with "current ongoing commercial negotiations", but that ministers want "clarity" on the plans for the retailer.
"It's absolutely legitimate for this government to ask the business if they're doing everything they can to protect employees and suppliers up and down the country," she added.
Dearden told MPs that the government would be ready to help the company's employees if Poundland collapses.
The head of Gordon Brothers' European operations reportedly told the government that the firm stood by its stewardship and had given Poundland £85m in additional financing since its purchase in 2025.

title: Kellogg's admits snap, crackle and pop is quieter after uproar over Rice Krispies recipe change
summary: The cereal giant has changed the recipes for Rice Krispies and Coco Pops, sparking a backlash online.
body:
Kellogg's has told the BBC the "snap, crackle and pop" sound made by its Rice Krispies may be noticeably quieter after an uproar over the cereal giant's recipe change.
Rice Krispies and Coco Pops are no longer being made with whole rice grains, with the tiny toasted puffs being made using corn flour and rice flour instead.
A Kellogg's spokesperson said retaining the iconic sound had been a "huge focus" when designing the new recipe, but that customers "might notice that the sound may be quieter and not as instant as before".
The firm was responding to complaints online that the taste of the breakfast staples had changed, with some fans adding they missed the "pop" sound.
Kellogg's said it had adapted the recipes due to "changing weather conditions" that have disrupted supplies of some grains and cereals.
The cereal giant said the new versions had been "carefully assessed for taste, appearance and texture", but some shoppers said their children would no longer eat them.
Some expressed dismay that the taste and texture were "totally different" and dubbed the change "grim" and "disgusting".
"There's no snap, crackle and pop in these," a parent named Dani wrote on TikTok. "My toddler won't eat them."
Lauren, also posting on TikTok, added that she had been eating Rice Krispies every day for breakfast "for years and years".
"I had a bowl of the new recipe and you can immediately tell the difference," she said. "They don't have the snapping sound when you put in the milk."
Jessicake meanwhile said they tasted "weird and stale".
The "Snap, Crackle and Pop" - made when milk is added to the puffed rice - has been a centrepiece of the brand's marketing since the 1950s.
Kellogg's insisted the snap, crackle and pop is "still there, but consumers might notice that the sound may be quieter and not as instant as before".
Recipe changes are notoriously difficult for big brands. Chocolate makers are constantly accused of reducing cocoa content in their products and debates rage online over whether ketchup ingredients have changed.
When Scottish fizzy drink Irn Bru cut its sugar content in 2018, fans famously stockpiled crates of the old version.
No changes are being made to Rice Krispies products in the US and Canada, which are owned by a separate company.
Kellogg's said the recipe change in the UK would help "maintain consistent quality" as extreme weather takes a toll on crops and pushes up ingredient prices.
Extreme weather in Spain in 2022 and 2023 in particular had reduced availability of the types of rice the company uses for its breakfast cereals, the company said
Rice Krispies, launched nearly a century ago, are sold around the world and come in variations such as vanilla and strawberry flavours in some markets alongside the widespread chocolate-flavoured Coco Pops version.
"We appreciate that even small changes to a much-loved product can feel noticeable and that's why we have approached this with a lot of care and consideration," Kellogg's said.
The firm said it appreciated the customer feedback and would "continue to look at ways to make [its] products even better in the future".
The cereals have already undergone some change, with reductions in salt content in the 1990s and lowered sugar in 2018. The company said Rice Krispies and Coco Pops will continue to meet UK food standards on levels of fat, salt and sugar in food.
A backlash against processed foods in recent years, especially those low in fibre and high in sugar, has put cereals generally under the spotlight from healthy eating advocates.
Kellogg's stressed the cereals contain no artificial colours, flavours or sweeteners and the nutritional benefits in each bowl, such as fibre, Vitamin D and iron are staying the same.
However, the new recipes mean packaging will now include a "contains wheat gluten" warning. It also continues to contain barley-malt extract.
Watch: How does El Niño affect world weather?
Kellogg's said it has not changed the recipe for any of its other cereals.
Many parts of the world have been affected by droughts, floods and heatwaves this year due to the El Niño weather phenomenon. The weather event is expected to severely affect crop production from South East Asia in particular. The region produces more than a quarter of the world's rice.
The World Meteorological Agency expects the record-breaking El Niño will last until at least 2027.
That will intensify pressure on food manufacturing companies, already looking at ways to source reliable and affordable ingredients.
The original Kellogg company separated into two distinct firms in 2023.
The largest is Kellanova, which focuses on snacks, cereals, noodles and other food products like Eggo, Pringles and Pop-Tarts sold globally. It is now owned by Mars, which makes confectionery and pet food.
The other business, WK Kellogg's, operates in North America and has since beentaken over by Italian chocolate giant Ferrero.

title: Time to focus on cost of living, says PM after US election results
summary: Andy Burnham says prices won't come down until the US's conflict with Iran is resolved.
body:
Watch: Andy Burnham reacts to US midterm results
Andy Burnham has said the results of the US midterm elections meant there was an "opportunity now to unite around the issue that is affecting us all, and that's the cost of living".
Speaking to broadcasters from the Commonwealth leaders summit, the prime minister promised to push for a resolution to the conflicts in the Middle East and Ukraine in the wake of the US elections that saw Donald Trump's Republicans suffer heavy losses.
He said he couldn't ease cost of living pressures until the US's conflict in Iran had been resolved.
Responding to the midterm results, the US president acknowledged that rising fuel prices - caused by the Iran war - had played a part in his party's defeats.
Speaking to Fox News, President Trump said: "People agree with what I'm doing on Iran but they really probably weren't willing to do the short term consequences of paying more for gasoline - I understand that."
Giving his reaction to the results, Burnham said the voters in the US have said they want to "see the world coming together and focusing on the things that matter to people".
Asked whether he thought the results might make the US president more unpredictable, Burnham said: "President Trump has accepted the results, and I feel the world has an opportunity now to unite around the issue that is affecting us all, and that's the cost of living.
"That has been the issue that I have put front and centre in my first three months in Downing Street, and we've made moves.
"But I can't get people's cost of living pressures down until the conflict in the Middle East is resolved, the conflict in Ukraine started by Russia.
"These are the things we have to focus on now, and I hope the world has a moment to do that.
"And certainly, in my calls with leaders, that is what I will be asking everybody to do."
Five reasons why Republicans lost so badly
Everything you need to know from the US midterm elections
The subject of the US midterm elections was raised at Prime Minister's Questions, which, in Burnham's absence, was taken by Cabinet Office Minister Louise Haigh.
The Liberal Democrat's deputy leader Daisy Cooper said American voters had rejected Trump's "warmongering and the economic chaos that it has caused".
She expressed concern that the US president was planning further strikes on Iran and urged the government to "stand together with our reliable allies and send a clear message to Trump and Netanyahu: there must be no more strikes."
Haigh replied: "The US are one of our most important allies and our priority absolutely is de-escalation."
She said the Iran war had been "catastrophic for the cost of living crisis" and said the Conservatives and Reform should "consider very carefully their judgment in calling for us to jump so readily into it".
Asked about suggestions there could be an attack on Iran in the coming week, Trumptold the Financial Times,externalon Tuesday: "The US was "locked and loaded if we need to go, but there may be no need for it".
Indirect talks between the two sides have been stalled for months and some analysts close to the Iran regime have suggested prolonging the negotiations, in the hope that the rising cost of fuel would damage Trump electorally.
Although the US Congress, now controlled by the Democrats, can restrict funding, Trump will still have significant authority over foreign policy.
Burnham is preparing a 10-year plan for government, and will be hoping that his strategy isn't blown off course by the actions of an unpredictable US president in his last two years in the White House.

title: Chris Mason: The US elections will change Trump - how will Burnham react?
summary: The big question for the British government is does defeat at home make it more likely that President Trump gets angrier abroad?
body:
The first public words from the prime minister after the American midterm elections were instantly revealing about contemporary international politics and diplomacy.
"Well, President Trump has accepted the results," Andy Burnham said.
It is not an observation British leaders have frequently had to make about recent American presidents – that they are not disputing the result of elections in their own country. But what would previously have been taken for granted no longer can be.
Burnham remains in the foothills of establishing a relationship with the president – so far it has amounted to a handful of phone calls andone face-to-face meetingat the United Nations in New York in September.
As he continues to attempt to build a rapport with Donald Trump, he will be doing so with a president in a wildly different political situation than when Sir Keir Starmer was trying to build bridges with him.
No longer is this a story of an extraordinary comeback, but of a midterm president seemingly punished for the consequences of a foreign war the type of which he had originally promised to avoid.
Time to focus on cost of living, says PM after US election results
Trump's loss limits powers at home, but it will likely be different abroad
And it is noticeable that the British government's public reaction is grounded too in the consequences of the war with Iran: the cost of living.
"I feel the world has an opportunity now to unite around the issue that is affecting us all and that's the cost of living," the prime minister said.
"But I can't get people's cost of living pressures down until the conflict in the Middle East is resolved, the conflict between in Ukraine started by Russia."
Within government the Iran war and its consequences, particularly on energy prices, is widely seen as the biggest individual contributor among the many factors currently driving up the cost of living.
And, bluntly, it is one that puts many, including many of America's allies, in alignment with many in America, Democrat and Republican, who when asked why these elections went as they did, point at the prices displayed outside any petrol station.
Speaking before the votes in America were counted, the Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband reflected on this when I spoke to himon BBC Newscast,external.
When I asked him specifically if he feared that a domestically humiliated Trump may prove more belligerent internationally, it was to the Iran war the foreign secretary referred.
He didn't offer a direct answer to my question, but chose instead to say this: "I know that one of the biggest responsibilities of the whole government, frankly, is the cost of living situation at home, and we know one of the biggest contributors to the cost of living situation is, frankly, the conflict."
"The Strait of Hormuz being not exactly closed, but not properly open, not free flowing, and that is hitting families at home," he said.
"We know that we need a diplomatic way out of this conflict, and so that is one of the things that we're working on. It's something I talked to the U.S. Secretary of State about at the G20, and it's something we continue to work on," he added.
The foreign secretary met Marco Rubio at the meeting in Atlanta last week.
But the big question for the British government, and so many others, is does defeat at home make it more likely that President Trump gets angrier abroad?
Or, do America's traditional allies, the UK, the European Union, Canada, Australia and others feel more strident and willing to work with Donald Trump's domestic political opponents to try to challenge and restrain a weakened president?
The answers to these two final questions will determine much in world affairs in the next couple of years.

title: Miliband says slavery apology will not bring cost for UK taxpayers
summary: Speaking to BBC's Newscast, the foreign secretary says Britain cannot sweep its past "under the carpet".
body:
Ed Miliband tells the BBC's Newscast podcast it is "right to confront this issue" of the transatlantic slavery trade
Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband has insisted the government's willingness to consider formally apologising for the UK's role in the transatlantic slave trade will not lead to higher costs for the British taxpayer.
Theprime minister has said the UK will not pay reparationsto affected countries, but declined to say whether his new approach could involve additional taxpayer money.
Speaking on the BBC's Newscast podcast, Miliband said previous British governments had a "sweep it under the carpet" attitude to the pain and consequences of slavery, citing what he described as former Prime Minister Sir Tony Blair's "sorry not sorry" remarks on the issue nearly two decades ago.
In 2007,Sir Tony said the UK's involvement in the slave tradewas a matter of "deep sorrow and regret".
"Tony Blair did sort of do a kind of sorry not sorry situation. He kind of expressed sorrow, and then said sorry, and then it was walked back by number 10," Miliband said.
Miliband said the former prime minister's approach was still referred to and came up in a recent conversation between Andy Burnham and the Prime Minister of Barbados Mia Mottley.
In addition, Miliband claimed, he and Burnham inherited a more recent mess, which is how the last Commonwealth Heads of Government Meeting (CHOGM) played out in Samoa two years ago.
Miliband said: "On the second day as my time as foreign secretary, I was told, 'look, one of your tasks is CHOGM 2024, which happened in Samoa, didn't go well.' To use sort of diplomatic speak, it ended up in a sort of punch up, a sort of verbal punch up about this whole issue."
He added: "This has really been hanging around as an issue for the Commonwealth for sort of 20 years, really. But it's grown and grown."
Given that, Miliband said, "we thought it was right to confront this issue and not to just try and sort of pretend that it didn't exist".
King calls slave trade a 'shameful chapter' during Commonwealth address
PM plans debt reset for Commonwealth nations as slavery apology talks begin
Burnham now says the government is open to formally apologising for slavery.
Ministers are beginning what they call a "structured dialogue" with affected countries, with the expectation that the apology may come at around the time the prime minister hosts the G20 Summit of world leaders in Manchester in November 2027.
"Is it weak to do this? I think it's the opposite of weak. I think fragile weak countries can't face up to their past. I'm really proud of Britain, but being proud of your country is also being willing to face up to things you didn't do, right?" Miliband said.
He said he had asked to be provided with a historical digest of the UK's involvement in the slave trade.
"Over three million people shipped, really with the British state's complicity, over a long period of time, couple of centuries actually, hundreds of thousands of them didn't make it and died," the foreign secretary said.
"Those who did make it had appalling conditions. Reading about the conditions on the ships and what happened to them when they arrived in the Caribbean and the Americas is really pretty harrowing."
Now he and the prime minister begin a process likely to formally apologise for this -and, they hope, create space for the Commonwealth to turn its attention to other things.
